headline: Conversation Rounds: Secret-Goal Role Play for ESL
problemStatement: A role play works best when both speakers have a reason to listen and respond. Conversation Rounds pairs two students in a generated situation and gives each a private goal on their phone. The rest of the class listens for useful phrases, so every learner has a job during the dialogue.
outcomes: Build fluency through short, goal-directed conversations rather than memorized scripts.
Practice listening for target phrases and noticing how classmates use them in context.
Give speakers feedback while encouraging every student to take part.
howItWorks: The activity selects a pair from students who have not spoken yet and gives each speaker a role card with a situation, goal, and useful phrases.
Speakers improvise the scene aloud. Their goals stay off the shared screen until the debrief unless the teacher chooses to reveal them.
Other students listen and tap phrases they hear on their phones. The teacher sees the count, and speakers can earn points for phrases the audience spots.
After the scene, the class reviews what happened and moves to another pair. Plot twists can add a new constraint while keeping the role-play moving.
teacherUseCases: Use one round to model how a phrase sounds in a real exchange before students practice it in pairs.
Run multiple rounds when the lesson needs broad participation; the activity tracks who has spoken and chooses a fresh pair.

faq.q: What do students see on their phones?
faq.a: The two speakers get their own role cards privately. Everyone else gets phrase-spotting controls so listeners can mark language they hear during the scene.

faq.q: Can classmates see the role goals?
faq.a: The goals stay hidden from the shared screen until the debrief by default. The teacher can reveal them if the class needs a clearer explanation of the scene.
The activity chooses from students who have not spoken yet, then tracks each pair's turns. This helps distribute speaking opportunities across the roster.

faq.q: What is the audience doing during a role play?
faq.a: Listeners hear the dialogue and tap the useful phrases they notice. Their selections appear as counts, turning audience attention into a language-listening task.
